items.title: Renters comfortably affording a house would need a $14,408 raise to buy one (October Rent Report)
items.description: Renters comfortably affording a house would need a $14,408 raise to buy one (October Rent Report) Rental demand is up 22% as buying a single-family home stretches the budget far further than renting one. Written by Kara Ng on November 12, 2026 A household that can comfortably afford to rent a single-family home would need a $14,408 annual raise to afford the monthly costs of owning a home. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, as measured by the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index, with demand for single-family rentals up 24.3%. The typical U.S. single-family rent was $2,243 a month in October, up 3.2% from a year ago, while the typical multifamily rent was $1,744, up 2.5%, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. Wanting a more suburban lifestyle — the extra space, yard and private garage that often come with a single-family home — doesn’t always mean stretching the budget to buy. In fact, it’s a stretch most families aren’t prepared to make, especially when a household comfortably affording the rent for a single-family home would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning one, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month. To comfortably afford those costs — the rule of thumb being to spend no more than 30% of its income on housing — a household needs an income of $89,724 to rent and $104,132 to buy. For many households, renting a house is a choice and not a fallback. It takes less income than owning, and it leaves more room in the monthly budget. The size of the raise depends on the market The pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise. Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs , according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline — the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead — at 7.8 years with 20% down. Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals. Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%. Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). items.title: OCTOBER CHILL BRINGS COOLER SALES, MORE CHOICES FOR HOUSTON BUYERS
items.description: OCTOBER CHILL BRINGS COOLER SALES, MORE CHOICES FOR HOUSTON BUYERS Home prices hold steady as supply reaches a 14-year high HOUSTON -- (November 11, 2026) -- The Greater Houston housing market saw a change in pace in October, offering buyers more choices while sellers adjusted to a shift in activity. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' October 2026 Housing Market Update, single-family home sales were 14.9% below last year's level, with 6,348 homes sold. The average home price held steady in October at $421,100, while the median price declined 3.0% to $320,000, its lowest level since January 2024. The number of homes on the market remained near record levels, with 40,253 single-family homes for sale, up 6.8% from last October. "Consumers are paying close attention to the economy and their household budgets, so it is understandable that some buyers are taking more time before purchasing a home," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "We typically see activity ease as the year winds down, but buyers who are still looking may have more time to find a home that fits their needs and budget." Housing Market Overview Across all property types, 7,485 properties were sold in October, down 15.1% compared with a year earlier. Total dollar volume dipped 14.6% to $3.06 billion. The number of active listings across all property types increased 4.8% to 61,965 Despite October's decline, single-family home sales through the first 10 months of 2026 remained within 2% of last year's pace. Stronger sales during the spring and early summer helped offset the declines recorded in recent months. Single-Family Homes Update In October, 6,348 single-family homes sold across the Houston area, compared with 7,458 during the same time last year. That represents a decline of 14.9%. October's single-family home sales were the fewest for any October in the past 10 years. However, total sales over the prior 12 months reached 87,433, remaining above the 2019 level of 85,685, the last normal year before the pandemic. The average price was virtually unchanged at $421,100. The median price was $320,000, which is 3.0% below last year's level. It is the lowest median price for any October since 2021, with an October peak of $335,000 in 2024. The average mortgage rate in October was 7.33%, up 108 basis points from a year ago, but still below the 7.62% recorded in October 2023. Buyers of a median-priced home paid an estimated monthly mortgage payment (including principal and interest) of $1,760.28. That is $134.79 more than a year ago but less than the $1,845.03 paid in October 2023, when both rates and median home prices were higher. "Affordability remains a challenge for homebuyers, and the possibility of a quarter-point interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve before the end of the year could add further pressure to the housing market," said HAR Chief Economist Ted C. Jones. Homes spent an average of 59 days on the market, unchanged from last October. Pending sales, which represent homes under contract but not yet sold, declined 17.6% to 6,445. The market had a 5.5-month supply of single-family homes, unchanged from September and its highest level since 2012. Nationwide, there was a 4.8 months' supply, according to the National Association of Realtors. Broken out by housing segments, single-family home sales performed as follows: $1 - $99,999: increased 2.1% (97 transactions) $100,000 - $149,999: decreased 1.0% (191 transactions) $150,000 - $249,999: decreased 9.4% (1,339 transactions) $250,000 - $499,999: decreased 16.8% (3,368 transactions) $500,000 - $999,999: decreased 16.9% (1,061 transactions) $1M and above: decreased 11.6% (291 transactions) HAR also reports on existing single-family home sales, which fell 10.2% in October. The average price declined slightly to $428,790, while the median price was down 4.5% to $315,000. HAR will publish its October 2026 Rental Market Update on Wednesday, November 18. For HAR's Monthly Activity Snapshot of the October 2026 trends, please CLICK HERE to access a downloadable PDF file. Townhome/Condominium Update The townhome and condominium market also recorded fewer sales in October. Sales declined 23.5% year over year, with 336 properties sold compared with 439 last October. The average sales price increased 5.8% to $263,413, while the median price declined 3.7% to $197,500. Active listings climbed 5.6% to 3,586 properties. The supply of townhomes and condominiums expanded from 8.2 months to 9.4 months, while days on market edged up to 65 days. Houston Real Estate Highlights in October Single-family home sales declined 14.9% year over year. Pending single-family sales declined 17.6% to 6,445. Active single-family listings increased 6.8% to 40,253. The average single-family home price was flat at $421,100. The median single-family home price declined 3.0% to $320,000, its lowest level since January 2024. Single-family homes took an average of 59 days to sell, unchanged from last year. The supply of single-family homes increased from 5.1 months to 5.5 months. Total property sales declined 15.1%, with 7,485 transactions. Total dollar volume declined 14.6% to $3.06 billion. items.title: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October
items.description: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October by Kim O'Brien Posted November 6, 2026 in Market Research October marked the first month of rent cuts in the U.S. apartment market in 2026, but annual gains continue at a robust pace. Same-store effective asking rents increased 1.7% year-over-year, according to October data from RealPage Market Analytics . That was the market’s biggest annual price increase since May 2023. While the annual reading has improved, the gain stemmed less from robust monthly pricing and more from weak rent performance falling out of the annual calculation. In fact, rents came down a mild 0.7% during October, marking the first monthly rent cut in the U.S. in calendar 2026. U.S. apartment occupancy faded to 95% in October, easing 20 basis points (bps) from the September showing. Still, October occupancy is up 40 bps in the calendar year and remains 10 bps ahead of the October 2025 showing. Helping support occupancy and rent performance, the U.S. apartment market has seen supply and demand edge closer to balance recently. Renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, gaining ground on a cooling supply wave. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units in the past year, nearly half the recent peak from late 2024. Bay Area and Midwest markets still lead for rent growth Rent performance remained sharply split by market. Coastal tech hubs and Midwest metros delivered the strongest annual gains, while most Sun Belt markets kept logging rent declines. Northern California's tech-driven markets posted the three strongest gains among the 50 largest apartment markets in the year-ending October. San Francisco saw rents hike 14.7% over the past year, San Jose followed at 9.5%, and Oakland reached 8.5%. All three markets are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest markets make up much of the rest of the top 10 list. Milwaukee led the major Midwest markets with annual rent growth of 4.2%, followed by Chicago (3.3%), Kansas City (3.1%) and Cleveland (3.1%). Detroit and St. Louis both fell just shy of making the cut, with annual rent growth of 2.7% in each market. Sun Belt rents still trail, but the gap is narrowing The South region overall has returned to annual rent growth, though barely, at 0.5% in October. Sun Belt and Florida markets continue to see the nation’s steepest declines. San Antonio had the deepest cut among big markets at 2.6%, stemming from occupancy at 92.5%, also dead last among the largest 50 markets. Also posting rent declines in the year-ending October were Houston (-1.8%), Tampa (-1%), Charlotte (-0.9%) and Denver (-0.8%). The bigger story, however, is how many Sun Belt markets have stopped seeing rent positioning hemorrhage. Annual increases have returned to Phoenix (0.4%) and Austin (0.6%), as well as Atlanta (0.8%), Raleigh (1.0%), Miami (0.6%) and Jacksonville (2.6%). WASHINGTON (November 12, 2026) – Existing-home sales decreased by 5.5% month-over-month and decreased by 8.8% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS® Existing-Home Sales report. The report provides the real estate ecosystem, including agents, homebuyers and sellers, with data on the level of home sales, price and inventory. Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West and held steady in the Northeast. Year-over-year sales declined in all four regions. “Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation. items.title: Members Of Congress Have Questions For Brookfield After Its Mass Mobile Home Purchase
items.description: Brookfield quietly closed on the acquisition of the largest privately held manufactured housing portfolio in the United States this year, prompting some members of Congress to inquire about the investment giant’s plans for the properties it now owns. Bisnow/Ethan Rothstein Brookfield purchased Yes Communities from GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, in the second quarter, public filings and statements from Brookfield management indicate. Brookfield hasn’t publicized its acquisition of the Denver-based operator of nearly 300 manufactured home developments, but three Democrats from the House of Representatives nonetheless sent a letter to the firm last month voicing concern about the purchase and seeking pledges for tenant protections. Reps. Maxwell Alejandro Frost, Gabe Vasquez and Rashida Tlaib asked management at New York-based Brookfield Asset Management, the publicly traded arm of Toronto-based Brookfield, and Brookfield Real Estate Group to provide assurances that residents’ quality of life wouldn’t be impacted by the deal. The representatives gave BAM until Nov. 20 to respond. The asset management giant hadn’t yet replied as of mid-November, Frost’s office confirmed to Bisnow on Nov. 9. Brookfield didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment. It hasn’t formally announced the acquisition, which was first rumored to be in the works in September 2025, but BAM said in second-quarter filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it acquired “the largest privately held U.S. manufactured home portfolio.” Yes Communities operates more than 55,000 housing sites across the U.S., with a focus on the Southwest, Midwest and Southeast. A purchase price for the portfolio is unknown, but BAM said it spent $5.2B in the second quarter on its real estate business, including the manufactured home portfolio and the take-private of an industrial outdoor storage portfolio. Brookfield announced a $1.2B all-cash deal in February to buy Peakstone Realty Trust, a REIT with 60 IOS properties and 16 traditional industrial assets. In its second-quarter filings, Brookfield Real Estate Income Trust disclosed a new investment in a 2% ownership interest in 294 manufactured housing properties at a book value of $86.6M, which aligns with the number of properties under the Yes Communities banner. BAM Chief Financial Officer Hadley Peer Marshall also disclosed on the second-quarter earnings call that a Brookfield fund had made its first investment by deploying capital to Yes Communities. Other affiliates of Brookfield may have also contributed capital for the Yes Communities acquisition. Brookfield REIT said in an investor presentation on its website that as of Sept. 30, it owned a 294-community manufactured housing portfolio across 23 states, the same number of states Yes Communities is active in. Wikimedia Commons; Office of Maxwell Frost Democratic Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Gabriel Vasquez and Maxwell Frost have asked Brookfield about its acquisition of Yes Communities. Executives from Brookfield held one virtual meeting with residents and their advocates following the acquisition that was facilitated by the Private Equity Stakeholder Project and MHAction, two nonprofit advocacy groups, PESP confirmed to Bisnow . GIC and another unnamed institutional investor acquired a 71% equity interest in Yes Communities in 2016, with Stockbridge Capital Group holding on to the remaining stake. Brookfield was reportedly in talks with GIC about acquiring its stake for more than $10B, and it is unclear exactly the size of Brookfield's interest in Yes Communities or how much it paid. In their letter from Oct. 13, the three members of Congress sought details about the acquisition. The letter outlines previous tenants' complaints with Yes Communities for high rent increases, excessive fees and neglect of routine maintenance and says that Brookfield “has the opportunity to change this scenario” and “support meaningful protections for its residents.” “Given the challenges our constituents have experienced at Yes! properties, as well as broader concerns about the private equity business model, we seek assurances that Brookfield will prioritize improving residents’ quality of life and protecting their economic and housing stability, rather than exacerbating the economic challenges they already face,” the representatives wrote. The letter specifically asks Brookfield to disclose whether it plans to increase rents by more than 3% annually, to outline its policy regarding new and existing fees, and to confirm whether it will refrain from serial eviction filings for routine rent collection. items.title: Rising rents draw Wall Street money to industrial outdoor storage lot investments across the U.S.
items.description: Hottest outdoor storage property markets The numbers help explain the appetite. Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses. Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically. The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial. Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025. Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots. "It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses," he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. "So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows," Cheema added. Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors. "Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it's hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios," Cheema said. Unlike traditional warehouses, there's no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. "That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there's still runway for small investors to find opportunities," Cheema said. "Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it's still largely local and regional banks," Cheema added. Zoning is the biggest challenge. "Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property's overall functionality," Sutterer said. For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. items.title: Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here's why
items.description: Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act 's institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels. According to the National Apartment Association ’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse , released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction , the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out. The industry's legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects. Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry. “I would say it hasn't normalized. In other words, it wasn't where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences , said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD . “I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.” Uncertainty is still taking a toll Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position. “Capital's coming in, but it's not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it's really hard for them to write checks. According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group , a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets. Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere. “When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn't have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview. Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29. "Capital's just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market's still trying to find itself,” Tanner said. In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern. “Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned. The uncertainty surrounding Treasury’s proposed rulemaking The U.S. Department of the Treasury , which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations. “If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, 'all right, built-to-rent is carved out.' But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said. Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy. Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued. The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects. Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban. items.title: The cost of 30 years of certainty
items.description: As mortgage rates top 7%, buyers increasingly turn to adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for monthly savings despite future reset risks. Upfront savings: A 5/1 ARM lowers initial rates by ~1%, saving ~$3,900 annually on a $500,000 loan. Volume surge: ARMs now account for 20% of mortgage dollar volume, led by high-cost states. Strong credit profile: Serious delinquency on post-2010 ARMs sits below 0.5%, proving more resilient than fixed-rate loans There is now a nearly $4,000 annual difference between paying for a $500,000 home with a fixed-rate mortgage and an adjustable-rate mortgage. That figure only grows alongside price. As affordability pushes buyers to make sacrifices, Cotality data shows that there’s been an increase in the number of buyers taking advantage of those extra funds afforded by adjustable-rate mortgages. The savings secured with these flexible mortgages is meaningful, but it’s not stable. “Buyers are taking a bet as affordability wears them down,” said Cotality Principal Economist Archana Pradhan, “They’re choosing available cash in the short term over a guarantee of consistent payments down the road. That solution has very market-dependent results.” An ARM to lean on Conventional wisdom has historically pushed buyers toward adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) when rates are rising. The thinking goes: lock in a rate for 5, 7, or 10 years and then refinance before the mortgage’s fixed period ends. That logic still holds appeal. With current mortgage rates above 7%, people taking out a conventional mortgage today will have a higher rate than most current homeowners; Cotality data shows only 28% of mortgages have interest rates above 5%. Taking out a 5-year ARM at current rates would drop a borrower’s interest rate down around a full point. Accordingly, a full 20% of mortgage dollar volumes are allocated to ARMs, according to Cotality data. However, if the rate adjusts upward following a fixed period, it can quickly eat away at earlier savings. And that reality is a distinct possibility. Cotality economists anticipate that current rates reflect a new normal rather than an anomaly. “Since the 2010s, rates have hovered around 2 to 5 basis points below where they are today. And then pandemic-era rates reset expectations to unrealistic levels,” said Pradhan. “People taking out ARMs today shouldn’t expect the rock-bottom-rates of 2020-2022 when they refinance down the road.” A refinance at the wrong time risks leaving someone exposed to larger monthly payments — and possible default. Buyers are taking a bet as affordability wears them down. They’re choosing available cash in the short term over a guarantee of consistent payments down the road. That solution has very market-dependent results. Archana Pradhan Cotality Principal Economist The price of popularity Affordability is pushing many buyers to the edge. Cotality tracks how homebuyers feel about price pressures , and in a recent survey , 69% of buyers said they were willing to cut lifestyle spending to afford a home. Sixty-five percent seek smaller mortgages for lower monthly payments. Buyers’ eagerness to take on ARMs underscores how strained they are; a few hundred dollars can make the difference between ending the month in the black or the red. items.title: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum
items.description: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 29, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Whether you call them “gateway” markets or the “sexy six,” the primary coastal hubs that traditionally attract the majority of domestic and international capital are well represented among the top markets for annual multifamily permitting in September’s data release from the U.S. Census Bureau, and in most cases are dramatically increasing their permitting activity. New York continues to lead the nation for multifamily permitting with 37,691 units permitted in the year-ending September, an increase of more than 13,000 units from last year or a jump of 52.7%. Los Angeles again ranked #2 with about 18,000 units permitted, almost doubling their annual total from one year ago. Washington, DC remained among the top permitting markets at #5 in September, increasing their annual permitting by 47.4% or about 3,900 units, while Seattle slipped to #11 this month but still increased their multifamily permitting total by 36.7% or roughly 2,400 units. Rounding out the “sexy six,” Boston ranked #16 among Realpage’s top 150 markets with a 44.7% annual increase (+2,303 units) to 7,460 units, while the Bay Area markets of San Jose, Oakland and San Francisco ranked well down the list individually but would have ranked #7 with a combined total of 11,543 units permitted, up 46.8% from last year (+5,407 units). Conversely, among the secondary high-growth markets, development activity has stalled or fallen back as top 10 markets Phoenix and Atlanta permitted close to the same amount as last year, while Dallas, Houston, Austin and Miami decreased their permitted unit counts by a combined 11,004 units. Only Raleigh/Durham saw a significant increase in multifamily permitting (+3,153 units) among the non-gateway top 10 markets. Despite declining permitting in four of September’s top 10 markets, their combined total of 148,456 units was up 14.5% from last September for an increase of 18,765 units. Compared to August, the top 10 markets’ annual permitting total was little changed (-0.7%). In addition to the expanding top 10 and the gateway markets mentioned, other markets with significant increases in annual units permitted in September were Kansas City (+2,187 units), West Palm Beach (+1,932 units), College Station-Bryan, TX (+1,762 units), Tacoma (+1,712 units) and Fort Worth (+1,672 units). Orlando (-4,572 units) led for annual permitting decreases, followed by Dallas and Houston. Significant decreases occurred in Columbus, OH (-2,911 units), Riverside-San Bernardino (-2,162 units), San Diego (-2,100 units) and Lakeland-Winter Haven, FL (-1,995 units). Permitting by Place Below the metro level, eight of August’s top 10 permit-issuing places returned to this month’s list with the first five remaining in order. The list of top individual permitting places (cities, towns, boroughs, and unincorporated counties) generally includes the principal city of some of the most active metro areas. The city of Los Angeles again led the nation for multifamily permitting at the local level with New York’s three most active boroughs returning among the top five. The city of Phoenix also placed in the top five while the city of Fort Worth jumped to #6 in September from #10 last month. The cities of Austin and Atlanta each slipped one spot as the cities of Columbus and Houston fell out of the top 10 entirely. The cities of Miami and Denver joined the top 10 list this month, permitting about 5,500 units apiece. Among the top 10 metros for multifamily permitting, Dallas, Houston, Washington, DC and Raleigh/Durham were not represented on the top 10 list of permitting places, although the core cities of Dallas, Houston, Raleigh and Durham were among the top 20 places. Washington, DC’s multifamily permitting was spread diversely around that metro’s area. items.title: VA default remains low despite record debt
items.description: Low default rates obscure record debt exposure across the expanding VA mortgage market. VA loans drive 9.5% of purchase originations, with average balances tripling to $418,000. Serious delinquency is low at 2.0% (vs. 5.0% for FHA), but record loan sizes amplify dollar risk. Zero-down financing and no monthly mortgage insurance make VA loans a vital hedge against high rates. Veterans are borrowing more money than ever before, and by conventional benchmarks, the VA loans asset class looks remarkably disciplined. According to Cotality data, delinquencies are sitting at a 2.0% — down from a year ago and roughly a third of the 6.5% pandemic peak, and well below the 5.0% recorded across the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) book. But a reassuring percentage can obscure an expensive reality. Low rates, record exposure The volume of distressed veteran mortgage debt is substantially larger than at any point in the last 20 years. In 2005, VA purchase loans were a niche product accounting for just 1.4% of purchase originations. Now they account for nearly ten times that number. VA purchase originations: Count and amount Data source: Cotality, 2026 One in every ten closed loans are VA-funded, which is actually down from their peak popularity in 2021 when VA originations surged near 282,000 loans, generating roughly $100 billion in volume across 2021 and 2022. But alongside the number of loans increasing, the average VA purchase balance has more than tripled, climbing from $122,500 in 1998 to $418,000 in 2026. When the pandemic-era competition recalibrated price ceilings, loan balances accelerated sharply from $286,000 to $355,000 in just two years. That popularity has mathematical consequences. A 2% delinquency on a portfolio of $122,500 loans comprising 1.4% of originations could be written off as an operational blip. But 2% delinquency on a $418,000 baseline across nearly a tenth of the national purchase market translates to billions in non-performing principal. Average VA purchase share by loan count Data source: Cotality, 2026 That risk isn’t due to borrowers failing at a higher rate. The size of VA loan portfolios has simply expanded to the point where small percentage slippages represent significant dollar exposure. Webinar Veteran Homeownership: Turning Service into Generational Wealth Affording stability This dramatic expansion in loan balances was not born of speculation, but of survival in a housing market where affordability is strained. With mortgage rates and home prices at near generational highs, the conventional path to homeownership is bending out of reach for millions . Accumulating a traditional 10% to 20% down payment on the national median home price of $429,450 demands $42,000 to $84,000 in liquid savings—a barrier that sidelines even buyers with comfortable earnings. Average VA purchase loan amount Data source: Cotality, 2026 ‍ A VA loan offers an achievable alternative. By offering loans with little to no downpayment requirement and eliminating monthly mortgage insurance requirements, this Ginnie Mae-backed option allows eligible service members and veterans to enter the market without draining cash reserves. When income shocks arrive, that liquidity buffer can keep families in their homes. That structural safety net is why VA loans crested at only 6.5% serious delinquency during the 2020 market tumult, while FHA loans spiked to 12.2% *. The defense corridors Because military demographics are highly geographic, this heavy-balance exposure is not even across the country, with clusters appearing in specific regional economies: Alaska: VA financing drives 28% of the funds put towards all home purchase originations. Virginia: VA loans account for 22% of the total dollar amount of all originations. Hawaii: VA transactions 20% of the total dollars that people put toward buying a home ‍ VA purchase dollar amount by state Data source: Cotality, 2026 In these markets, the VA loan is the bedrock of local housing turnover. Any shift in federal loan limits, interest rate trajectories, or military deployment cycles triggers an outsized local shock. The VA loan has become a high-balance, high-volume credit engine. For mortgage originators and servicers, the payment discipline of this population offers security, but the larger loan sizes mean there is far less margin for error when local job markets or regional housing valuations stumble. For servicers and secondary-market investors managing these pools, the priority is no longer just tracking the headline delinquency rate. It is managing the sheer weight of the capital behind it. Webinar Veteran Homeownership: Turning Service into Generational Wealth *The CARES Act provided forbearance for borrowers with federally backed mortgage loans who were economically impacted by the pandemic. Borrowers in a forbearance program who have missed a mortgage payment are included in the Cotality delinquency statistics, even if the loan servicer has not reported the loan as delinquent to credit repositories Property market economics Mortgage banking & financial technology Housing affordability

items.title: October 2026 CPI: Inflation Firms, December Fed Hike Looms
items.description: October 2026 CPI: Inflation Firms, December Fed Hike Looms By Jake Krimmel Nov 10, 2026 October's consumer price index came in a touch hotter than forecasters expected, with headline inflation up 0.4% on the month and core up 0.3%. Because of last year's government shutdown, BLS did not publish annual rates, but the details show inflation remains broad-based. December Fed hike odds jumped to 99% and the 10-year Treasury yield moved higher, putting new upward pressure on mortgage rates after three straight weekly declines. Here's what today's report means for the Fed, consumers, and the housing market. October 2026 CPI at a Glance Headline CPI: +0.4% MoM Seasonally Adjusted (SA), following September's +0.6% rise, versus forecasts of +0.2% to +0.3%; BLS did not publish an annual rate because October 2025 data were not collected during the government shutdown Core CPI (less food & energy): +0.3% MoM (SA), matching September and August, versus a forecast of +0.2% Energy: +0.7% MoM (SA) after +5.2% in September; gasoline +1.0% MoM (SA) and +37.4% YoY Food: +0.5% MoM (SA), with food at home up 0.4% and food away from home up 0.5% Shelter: +0.3% MoM (SA) after +0.4% in September, with rent up 0.2% and owners' equivalent rent up 0.3% Real earnings: real average hourly earnings were unchanged, as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation Fed outlook: odds of a December hike jumped to 99%, with Governor Waller's comments putting a 50 basis point move on the table Market reaction: the 10-year Treasury yield was up 9 basis points 25 minutes after the release Mortgage rates: Freddie Mac's 30-year rate fell to 7.18% in the week of November 5, the third straight weekly decline, after peaking at 7.4% in October October CPI: a touch hotter than expected, and inflation remains broad-based October’s CPI came in a touch hotter than consensus, with headline up 0.4% month over month (versus a forecasted 0.2 to 0.3%) and core inflation rising 0.3% month over month compared to an expected 0.2%. These figures hardly qualify as a shock to markets or the outlook, but the details of the report show inflation remains broad-based, with food, energy, shelter, and vehicles all up, to name a few. The BLS did not publish annual rates because of last year’s government shutdown, but headline inflation likely remains in the high 3s. These are the costs most salient to consumers and voters, as we saw, yet the Fed has less direct control over them. What it means for the Fed: a December hike looks almost certain The same supply-side and geopolitical pressures are still at work, with energy playing an important role and tariff-driven goods inflation not going away. These are the costs most salient to consumers and voters, as we saw, yet the Fed has less direct control over them. On the Fed outlook, a December hike now looks almost certain, with odds jumping to 99% this morning . That market reaction is both due to the warmer than anticipated CPI print and Governor Waller’s comments (which occurred prior to the CPI report) putting a 50 basis point move on the table for December. Additional hikes in early 2027 look more in play as well, with the 10-year Treasury up 9 basis points just 25 minutes after the CPI report release. What it means for housing: mortgage rates could turn higher again For housing in the near term, we could see upward pressure on mortgage rates again. After three straight weekly declines to 7.18% , rising Treasury yields and growing speculation about hikes in early 2027 could reverse that trend. October’s spike to 7.4% showed how quickly higher rates hurt demand, with contract signings and new listings each falling about 10% from September as buyers and sellers pulled back . Rate swings grab the headlines and matter for the marginal buyer, but the real wage squeeze is a longer-run, underexplored headwind for demand. Real average hourly earnings were flat in October as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation, leaving annual real wage growth negative for buyers already facing mortgage rates above 7% .

items.title: October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices
items.description: October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices Published on November 10th, 2026 by Dana Anderson The median U.S. home-sale price fell in October for the first time in over 3 years. Prices are still rising rapidly in some metros with hot markets, including San Francisco, where they rose 16.8% year over year, and the greater New York City area. Home sales fell as mortgage rates surpassed 7%–but flattening prices could bring buyers a bit of relief. Would-be sellers are starting to pull back as demand declines, but the total number of homes for sale climbed to its highest level since 2020. For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended. The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year , even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023. With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices. Home Prices Are Still Rising Fast in Hot Markets, Led By San Francisco Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County. In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market. Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand . U.S. Pending Home Sales Drop to Lowest Level Since the Pandemic National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020. This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33% , a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before. All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here . “It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.” Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier. items.title: The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math
items.description: The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math Published on November 12th, 2026 by Dana Anderson , Yingqi Xu and Szu Yu Chen Timing made a big difference for millennials. Those who bought a home before 2022 locked in historically low mortgage rates. But those who bought after rates and prices surged spent about 35% of their income on housing–and many other millennials were priced out entirely. Baby boomers had a brutal start, with double-digit mortgage rates in the early 1980s, but falling rates gave them decades to refinance. When boomers were in their late 30s, they spent just over 25% of their income on housing. The typical monthly payment was about $3,000 when elder millennials were 40 to 44 (2021 to 2025), versus about $1,986 for boomers at those ages, in today’s dollars. Millennials earn more than boomers did at the same age in today’s dollars, partly because more women are in the workforce, but housing costs more than cancel out the difference. If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home . For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent. The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation. Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000. Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments. This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology. Millennials Had an Early Homebuying Advantage In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb. Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage. Then the Math Changed The millennial advantage didn't last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income. items.title: Household Debt Delinquencies Rise as Mortgage Performance Weakens
items.description: Household Debt Delinquencies Rise as Mortgage Performance Weakens November 11, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Household debt delinquency rates increased in the third quarter of 2026 as the share of delinquent balances and the transition to seriously delinquent debt increased. According to the latest Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, about 5.0% of outstanding household debt balances were in some stage of delinquency, an increase of 0.3 percentage points (pp) from the previous quarter. Total household debt balances that were seriously delinquent (at least 90 days delinquent) also edged up slightly from 3.3% in the second quarter to 3.4%. The deterioration occurred across several consumer loan categories. The serious delinquency rate for auto loans increased 0.2 pp to 5.7%, while mortgage delinquency rate increased 0.1 pp to 1.1%. In contrast, the serious delinquency rate for credit cards edged lower to 12.9%, although credit cards continued to have the highest rate among the major debt categories. Student loans displayed continued deterioration. The share of student loan balances that were seriously delinquent increased to 10.9%, from 10.6% in the second quarter. This marked a further increase in the proportion of student loan debt classified as seriously delinquent following the resumption of delinquency reporting. The flow of balances newly entering a serious delinquency stage showed a more mixed picture. Overall, 2.6% transitioned into serious delinquency during the third quarter, unchanged from the previous quarter. The share of student loan balances transitioning into serious delinquency declined to 7.7%, from 7.8% in the previous quarter. This followed a much sharper decline in the second quarter, when the transition rate dropped from 10.9% to 7.8%. Credit card transitions also improved slightly. The share of credit card balances newly entering serious delinquency decreased to 6.9%, from 7.0% in the second quarter, marking the third consecutive quarterly decline. Mortgage transitions, however, continued to move in the opposite direction. The share of mortgage balances newly entering serious delinquency increased to 1.6%, from 1.5% in the previous quarter. This category has been gradually trending upward in recent years, indicating continued deterioration in mortgage credit performance. Auto loan transitions remained relatively steady at 3.0%. Columbia Senior Attorney - Arizona or New Mexico Explore More Job Openings U.S. Treasury’s Proposed Regulations Concerning Title X Of The 21st Century ROAD To Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know by: John Cagigas , Winstead - News Alert Monday, November 9, 2026 Related Practices & Jurisdictions Real Estate Financial Institutions Banking Administrative Regulatory All Federal Print Mail Download />i Introduction On July 11, 2026, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 19521 (the “ Act ”). As discussed in our June 24 article, “Title X of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know” (the “ Initial Article ”), Title X of the Act generally bars a “ large institutional investor ” from buying—or entering into a contract to buy—a “ single-family home ” unless a statutory exception applies. Under the Act, a covered investor must be a qualifying for-profit entity engaged in the single-family rental (“ SFR ”) business that, alone or with others acting “ in concert ,” has direct or indirect “ investment control ” over at least 350 single-family homes. Homes acquired through statutory exceptions after July 11, 2026, are excluded from that count. For this purpose, a “ single-family home ” generally means a structure with no more than two dwelling units, excluding manufactured homes. On October 23, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury (the “ Treasury ”) issued proposed regulations under Title X (proposed 31 C.F.R. Part 36, the “ Proposed Regulations ”). The Proposed Regulations explain several exceptions for build-to-rent (“ BTR ”), renovate-to-rent, homeownership programs, creditor enforcement and institutional resales, as well as rules affecting investment funds and managers. However, some of the Treasury’s proposals could also complicate common BTR development and sale structures. As of the date hereof, the Proposed Regulations are not binding or final, and the Treasury expects additional rulemakings. Public comments on the Proposed Regulations will be due by November 23, 2026, and the statutory purchase prohibition under the Act becomes effective January 7, 2027, independent of when final regulations are adopted. Key Takeaways The headline for BTR is mixed: the Treasury proposes a purchase deadline of 18 months after a home receives its certificate of occupancy, but also confirms that qualifying homes can be resold repeatedly between covered institutional investors. The Treasury also proposes a written-program requirement for several exceptions and a more detailed test for passive investors. Important gaps remain that are unresolved in the Proposed Regulations, including how the Act applies to fund aggregation, equity transfers, pre-effective-date purchase contracts and BTR homes leased before an institutional sale. The discussion below distinguishes what Congress expressly provided in the Act from the additional conditions the Treasury now offers in the in the Proposed Regulations. BTR Protection: Greater Certainty, but a Narrower Initial Acquisition Window The Act expressly allows purchases under a BTR program in which a large institutional investor “ purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains ” newly constructed homes to be managed as rentals. Our Initial Article explained why that language appeared to protect traditional BTR development and institutional takeout sales. The Treasury’s proposed definition, however, focuses on when a home is purchased and how it is first occupied. Proposed § 36.5 would require a home acquired under the BTR exception to (i) have no previous owner-occupant, (ii) be purchased within 18 months after its certificate of occupancy (or local equivalent), and (iii) be first occupied by renters after the purchase. The Treasury rejected an alternative that would treat an older home as “ newly constructed ” solely because it was originally built and continuously used as a rental. The proposal does not separately explain how these purchase-focused requirements apply when an institutional investor itself constructs and retains the homes, a scenario the Act expressly includes. This may matter for merchant-builders that deliver a community in phases, lease homes as they are completed and sell the stabilized project in one transaction. Because the proposed deadline is tied to each home’s certificate of occupancy, earlier phases could fall outside the proposed BTR exception even while later phases qualify. The Treasury has not proposed a project-wide extension measured from the final phase or stabilization. Another statutory exception may be needed for homes that miss the 18-month window. A second issue concerns lease-up before closing. The proposed § 36.5(c) states that homes must be “ after the purchase, first occupied by renters .” That language appears to require that first-time rental occupancy occur after the institutional buyer purchases the homes, so a home already renter-occupied before sale would appear ineligible for this exception. The Proposed Regulations do not expressly disqualify pre-leased homes or analyze pre-sale lease-up, so clarification remains warranted before buyers rely on this exception. The Act permits BTR homes in both entirely rental and mixed rental/owner-occupied communities, and the Treasury confirms that the exception is not lost simply because a development also contains other property types. The rule still applies home-by-home: conventional apartment buildings with three or more dwelling units per structure generally fall outside the Act’s definition of “ single-family home ,” while qualifying SFR homes within the same development remain subject to the applicable exception. items.evidence_quote: Treasury’s Proposed Regulations Concerning Title X Of The 21st Century ROAD To Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know by: John Cagigas , Winstead - News Alert Monday, November 9, 2026 Related Practices & Jurisdictions Real Estate Financial Institutions Banking Administrative Regulatory All Federal Print Mail Download />i Introduction On July 11, 2026, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 19521 (the “ Act ”). As discussed in our June 24 article, “Title X of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know” (the “ Initial Article ”), Title X of the Act generally bars a “ large institutional investor ” from buying—or entering into a contract to buy—a “ single-family home ” unless a statutory exception applies. Under the Act, a covered investor must be a qualifying for-profit entity engaged in the single-family rental (“ SFR ”) business that, alone or with others acting “ in concert ,” has direct or indirect “ investment control ” over at least 350 single-family homes.

executive_summary.text: NAR 报告显示，10 月成屋销售环比下降 5.5%、库存增加；30 年期房贷利率虽连降四周至 7.11%，仍高于上年同期，Realtor.com 提示通胀再添利率上行压力。Zillow 显示独栋租赁需求同比增长 24.3%，但 HousingWire 指出，BTR 即使获得法定豁免，实施规则及新增立法的不确定性仍压制资本流入。RealPage 指出公寓年度租金改善主要受基数影响，10 月租金与入住率均回落，运营复苏仍待观察。
executive_summary.text_en: NAR reported October existing-home sales fell 5.5% monthly as inventory rose. The 30-year mortgage rate fell for a fourth week to 7.11% but remained above a year earlier; Realtor.com flagged renewed inflation-driven rate pressure. Zillow showed single-family rental demand rose 24.3% annually, but HousingWire reported that implementation and legislative uncertainty still constrain BTR capital despite statutory exemptions. RealPage attributed improving annual apartment rent growth mainly to base effects; October rents and occupancy declined, leaving an operating recovery unconfirmed.
